stances.claim: Filipinos have a native, indigenous concept of justice (katarungan), not borrowed from the West -- its root tarong means 'straight, upright, appropriate, correct,' tying justice to moral rectitude and right action rather than mere legality.
stances.rhetorical_move: etymological-sovereignty argument (using language to establish cultural authenticity)

stances.claim: Filipino language is more discriminating than European languages on the concept of justice: where Spanish/Italian/French/German conflate 'right' and 'law,' Tagalog distinguishes karapatan (right) from batas (command/law), recognizing that what is legal may not always be just.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-linguistics framing (using European conflation as foil for Filipino precision)

stances.claim: The fundamental element of Filipino justice is fairness; privilege (pribelehiyo -- Spanish loanword) and naked power (poder, lakas -- distinct from legitimate kapangyarihan) are alien to the Filipino mind, evidenced by the borrowed/native word boundary.
stances.rhetorical_move: loanword-vs-native-word argument (using lexical provenance as evidence of cultural attitude)

stances.claim: Filipino history puts 'flesh' on the linguistic 'bones' -- a continuous struggle against Spanish, American, Japanese invaders and the Marcos dictatorship demonstrates an unbending Filipino intent to create a just society.
stances.rhetorical_move: bones-and-flesh dual-method (language + history as twin proofs)

stances.claim: Filipino social justice has five elements: (1) respect for rights, (2) repair of injustices to the poor, (3) self-sustaining economy distributing benefits to all, (4) institutional change so inequalities are not produced by institutions/structures (unless temporarily favoring the least favored at the most-favored's cost), and (5) means capable of attaining these objectives.
stances.confidence: asserted via Diokno as authoritative thesis

notable_anecdotes: Diokno's root-word analysis -- tarong (Visayan, root of katarungan) = straight/upright/appropriate/correct -- the etymology functions as the column's primary argument, the rare opinion column where a single word's root carries the philosophical thesis.

The lexical asymmetry: karapatan (right) is native Filipino, but pribelehiyo (privilege) is a Spanish loanword -- Diokno reads the borrowed/native boundary as evidence that Filipinos historically had no concept of privilege as legitimate, which is the single sharpest cultural-philosophical move in the lecture.
Ka Pepe's bones-and-flesh metaphor for language and history as the dual sources of the Filipino concept of justice -- the structural device that organizes the entire column.

The fifth element of Diokno's social-justice definition -- institutional change so that inequalities are not caused by institutions -- with the qualifier that inequality may be temporarily acceptable only if it favors the least favored at the cost of the most favored, a Rawlsian difference principle stated in Filipino voice.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban devotes his column to Dean Jose Manuel I. Diokno's lecture as one of the 10 CJ Panganiban Professorial Chair holders on Liberty and Prosperity, asking whether justice is an imported Western concept or whether Filipinos have a native one. Citing his father Sen. Jose W. 'Ka Pepe' Diokno, Diokno argues that Filipinos have katarungan, whose root tarong (Visayan) means 'straight, upright, appropriate, correct' -- making justice for Filipinos a matter of moral rectitude and right action, not mere legality. Karapatan (right) shares the root dapat (fitting, appropriate), tying justice to right; batas (law) merely means command. Unlike Spanish/Italian/French/German, which conflate 'right' and 'law,' Tagalog distinguishes the two, recognizing that what is legal may not always be just. Kapangyarihan (authority) is differentiated from poder and lakas (naked power), and karapatan (native, right) from pribelehiyo (Spanish loanword, privilege) -- with the loanword/native boundary itself read as evidence that privilege and naked power are alien to the Filipino mind. Ka Pepe likened language to the 'bones' and history to the 'flesh': Filipino history's continuous resistance to Spanish, American, Japanese, Marcos and US-bases impositions provides the historical struggle that puts flesh on the linguistic bones. Diokno closes with a five-element definition of Filipino social justice: (1) respect for rights, (2) repair of injustices to the poor, (3) self-sustaining economy distributing benefits, (4) institutional change so that inequalities are not caused by institutions (unless temporarily favoring the least favored at the most-favored's cost -- a Rawlsian difference principle in Filipino voice), and (5) means capable of attaining these objectives. Panganiban closes by previewing the next installment: does our current justice system reflect this concept?
